dewaal-smart-animals.author: Frans de Waal
dewaal-smart-animals.intro: The primatologist Frans de Waal looks back on a century of change in the study of animal cognition: from treating animals as stimulus–response machines to recognizing that each species has its own kind of intelligence. His central position is **evolutionary continuity**: the mental differences between humans and other animals are differences of degree, not of kind.

roach-stiff.author: Mary Roach
roach-stiff.intro: Science journalist Mary Roach tours dissecting rooms, a body farm where corpses are left to decay, crash-test labs and crematoriums to chronicle the "second career" cadavers have in science: practice for surgeons, crash tests, help in solving air disasters, even experiments to locate the soul. The tone is brisk and funny, but never loses its respect for the dead. **The core attitude**: death itself is sad, but a body that has already died need not just lie there; it can still do something useful.

greene-hidden-reality.author: Brian Greene
greene-hidden-reality.intro:
String theorist Brian Greene examines, one by one, the **nine kinds of parallel universe** that have emerged from modern physics: copies of us in infinite space, bubble universes spawned endlessly by inflation, string theory's brane worlds and landscape, the many worlds of quantum mechanics, the holographic universe, and finally simulated universes and the idea that "all possible mathematics exists".

His stance is restrained: **none has been confirmed**, and he himself is not convinced; but none of these ideas is idle fantasy. Each emerges "unbidden" from theories developed to explain the data we already have. The book's other through-line is a question: can a universe we can never see still count as science?

henderson-barely-imagined.author: Caspar Henderson
henderson-barely-imagined.intro:
In homage to Borges's *Book of Imaginary Beings*, the British journalist Caspar Henderson picks, from **A to Z**, 27 animals that **really exist** yet are stranger than mythical monsters: the axolotl that regrows its limbs, the sponge with no organs, the mantis shrimp that punches like a bullet, the tardigrade that can survive in space...

Each chapter starts from one animal and wanders freely into myth, history, philosophy, art and humanity itself. Three threads run through the book: **evolution** is more wondrous than myth; the **ocean** is the home we know least (about two-thirds of the book's subjects come from the sea); and, in the Anthropocene, how we should treat these vanishing lives.

levesque-last-stargazers.author: Emily Levesque
levesque-last-stargazers.intro:
The author is an astronomer at the University of Washington who studies how **massive stars** (red supergiants in particular) live and die. This book is not about astronomical knowledge as such but about **people**: how astronomers climb remote mountaintops and stay up all night at the telescope, turning light that set out millions of years ago into data. She interviewed more than a hundred colleagues for it and gathered a trove of outrageous, funny and moving observing stories.

The "last" in the title refers to this: "classical observing", going up the mountain in person and sitting in the control room all night, is being replaced by automated queue observing, remote observing and sky surveys. This way of working, and the whole culture it produced (the superstitions, the playlists, the night lunches, the car-crash tradition), may disappear along with this generation.

The book: an introduction plus thirteen chapters, running roughly from the author's first trip up a mountain to observe, through weather, volcanoes, gunfire, telescopes on airplanes and gravitational waves, all the way to "supernovae in your inbox" and the future of automated surveys.

ishiguro-klara-sun.author: Kazuo Ishiguro
ishiguro-klara-sun.intro:
Published in 2021, Kazuo Ishiguro's first novel after his Nobel Prize, dedicated to his mother, who had died the year before. The narrator, **Klara**, is an AF (Artificial Friend), a solar-powered robot bought as a companion for a child. From a shop window she meets the frail teenager **Josie**, is taken home, and turns all her powers of observation on this household, this child, and a world she only ever sees from the side.

Klara believes the **Sun** is a being with a will who can grant favours, because she herself runs on his 'nourishment'. The whole book is a machine bringing a mistaken theology and a true love to bear on something humans themselves dare not look at directly.

Six parts: **Part One** in the store; **Part Two** at Josie's house, meeting Rick the neighbour boy, the trip to Morgan's Falls; **Part Three** Josie's illness worsens and Klara begins her secret plan; **Part Four** the city; **Parts Five and Six** are short and form the ending.

The English is very simple. The challenge is **Klara's point of view**: she gives things capitalised names (*the Mother, Manager, Beggar Man, the RPO Building*), 'estimates' people's ages, and her vision splits into boxes when emotions run high. She always sees more than she understands; the reader's work is to fill in, under her calm narration, what she leaves unsaid. The guides try not to spoil what comes later.

Note: the novel is divided only into six parts, with scene breaks inside each. Here each part is cut by plot into sections for the guides (the titles are our summaries), and 'Read the original' extracts the matching passage.

vance-dying-earth.author: Jack Vance
vance-dying-earth.intro: Jack Vance's first book (1950): six linked stories set on Earth in its last age, when the sun is a dim red ember and science has dwindled into a few memorized spells. Wizards grow people in vats, witches hold Sabbaths, and man-eating Deodands and dragonfly-riding Twk-men roam the forests. The book founded the 'dying Earth' subgenre and influenced writers such as Gene Wolfe and George R. R. Martin; its spells that are memorized and forgotten once cast became 'Vancian magic' in Dungeons & Dragons. Characters reappear across the stories, so you'll keep recognizing earlier faces. Vance's English is ornate, precise and ironic, full of rare or invented words: don't look them all up, just enjoy the rhythm. 15 guide sections; the longer stories are split. Content note: torture, attempted sexual assault, sexualized ritual and thoughts of suicide, mostly in stories 3 and 4.

lindsay-arcturus.author: David Lindsay
lindsay-arcturus.intro:
The first and best-known novel by **David Lindsay** (1876–1945). Almost ignored in his lifetime, it later became a 'hidden classic' of fantastic and philosophical fiction; C. S. Lewis said it influenced his Space Trilogy.

After a séance in London, the rough and mysterious Krag takes Maskull to **Tormance**, a planet of Arcturus. Everywhere he goes his body grows new organs and he meets a new morality: Joiwind's selfless love, Oceaxe's will, Spadevil's duty, the metaphysics of the phaens, the painful love of Lichstorm... Each is beautiful, and each is poisonous. In the end he discovers that pleasure and beauty may be the deceptions of the creator **Crystalman**, while pain (Krag) is the guide to the real (**Muspel**).

**How to read it**: like a dreamlike road novel, with a new world every two or three chapters. Don't worry about understanding every invented name; treat it as a journey of the senses and of morals. **Content note**: a great deal of violence and death.

10 guide sections, each covering 2–3 chapters.

**Edition note**: the book is part of the collection *Four Novels*. All four share one epub file; the first time you open the original, choose that collection file.

huff-lie-statistics.author: Darrell Huff
huff-lie-statistics.intro:
A short book from 1954 by **Darrell Huff** (1913–2001), illustrated with cartoons by Irving Geis, and one of the best-selling books on statistics ever written. Huff wasn't a statistician but a journalist and editor, so it reads like a collection of witty magazine columns.

The title is ironic. Huff pretends to teach you how to fool people with numbers: pick a flattering sample, choose a convenient average, hide the error and the range, chop the bottom off your chart, pass off correlation as cause... one trick per chapter. Read in reverse, it's **a self-defence manual against statistical lies**. The last chapter gives you five questions to carry around.

**How to read it**: the English is plain and conversational, full of American wisecracks, and needs almost no maths. The examples (prices, magazines, ads, polls) come from the 1940s and '50s; some are dated, and some phrasing wouldn't pass today. But every one of the tricks still turns up daily in news, advertising, company reports and social media. Try matching each chapter with an example from today.

**Note**: many of the arguments depend on the illustrations (line graphs, moneybags, cows). The images in the e-book may be small, so zoom in when needed.

Ten guides: the Introduction and Chapter 1 together, then one per chapter, with Chapter 10's five sections in one guide.
